title: Reentrancy in withdraw allows draining the vault via ERC777 hooks
body: The withdraw function transfers the underlying token to msg.sender before it decrements the caller share balance. When the underlying is an ERC777 token the transfer triggers the tokensReceived hook on the recipient, which re-enters withdraw while the stale balance is still recorded. An attacker can loop the callback until the vault is drained. The checks-effects-interactions ordering is violated: state mutation must happen before any external call, and a nonReentrant guard should wrap the entry point.

title: Spot price from Uniswap V2 reserves is trivially manipulable by a flash loan
body: getPrice reads reserve0 and reserve1 directly from the Uniswap V2 pair and divides them to obtain a spot price. Reserves are mutable within a single transaction, so an attacker can flash borrow, skew the pool, call borrow against the inflated collateral price, and unwind in the same transaction. The protocol should consume a time weighted average price over a window of several blocks, or a Chainlink aggregator with staleness and deviation checks, and never a raw reserve ratio.

title: Chainlink answer consumed without staleness or bounds validation
body: The adapter calls latestRoundData but discards updatedAt, answeredInRound and roundId, and does not require answer to be strictly positive. If the feed halts, or a round is incomplete, the protocol keeps pricing collateral against a frozen quote. During the LUNA depeg several aggregators pinned at their minAnswer circuit breaker, so borrowers could keep drawing against a price the market no longer honoured. Validate updatedAt against a heartbeat, require answer above zero, and revert on answeredInRound below roundId.

title: Missing access control on initialize allows anyone to seize the proxy
body: The implementation contract exposes initialize as a public function with no initializer modifier and no constructor call to _disableInitializers. Any account can front run deployment, call initialize on the proxy and set itself as owner, gaining authority over the upgrade path and the fee recipient. Mark the function with the OpenZeppelin initializer modifier, invoke _disableInitializers in the implementation constructor, and atomically initialize inside the deployment transaction.

title: First depositor can inflate share price and steal later deposits
body: When totalSupply is zero the vault mints shares equal to the assets deposited. The first depositor mints one wei of shares, then donates a large amount of the underlying directly to the vault contract, inflating assets per share. A subsequent depositor whose deposit is smaller than the inflated share price receives zero shares because of the floor division, and their assets accrue to the attacker. Mitigate with virtual shares and virtual assets in the conversion, or by minting dead shares to address zero at deployment.

title: Rounding direction favours the user in previewWithdraw
body: convertToShares rounds down in both the deposit and the withdraw path. ERC-4626 requires that share arithmetic always round in favour of the vault: shares minted on deposit round down but shares burned on withdraw must round up. Because the withdraw path rounds down, a user repeatedly withdrawing dust extracts one wei more of the underlying than they are entitled to on each call, and the loss accrues to the remaining depositors.

title: Signature replay across chains because chainId is absent from the digest
body: The message digest is keccak256 over the recipient, amount and nonce, but omits block.chainid and the verifying contract address. A withdrawal proof signed by the validator set on one chain therefore verifies unchanged on every other chain where the same bridge is deployed, letting an attacker replay a legitimate release to mint a second time. Bind the digest to an EIP-712 domain separator containing name, version, chainId and verifyingContract, and cache it against a chainId change to survive a fork.

title: ecrecover return value not checked against the zero address
body: verifySignature compares the address returned by ecrecover to a stored signer without first rejecting the zero address. Malformed signature parameters make ecrecover return the zero address, so if the signer slot is ever unset, or a mapping lookup misses, the comparison succeeds for an arbitrary signature. The contract also accepts s values in the upper half of the curve order, admitting a second malleable encoding for every valid signature. Use the OpenZeppelin ECDSA recover helper, which reverts on both conditions.

title: Unbounded loop over stakers makes reward distribution griefable
body: distributeRewards iterates the full stakers array and writes to storage in each iteration. Because anyone can stake the minimum amount, an attacker can register thousands of dust positions until the loop exceeds the block gas limit, after which distribution reverts permanently and no participant can be paid. Replace the push distribution with a pull accumulator: track a rewardPerTokenStored index, update it in constant time, and let each staker settle their own accrual on claim.

title: Reward accounting uses transferred amount rather than balance delta
body: stake credits the caller with the amount argument, but a fee on transfer or rebasing token delivers less than the amount requested. The vault therefore over credits the depositor and, once several such positions unwind, the last withdrawers cannot be paid because the recorded liabilities exceed the actual balance. Measure the balance before and after the transferFrom and credit only the observed delta, or maintain an explicit allow list of standard ERC-20 tokens.

title: Swap does not enforce a minimum output, exposing users to sandwich attacks
body: swapExactTokensForTokens forwards a minOut of zero to the router and has no deadline argument. A searcher observing the pending transaction can front run it to move the pool, let the victim execute at the worse price, and back run to close the position, capturing the difference. Every swap path must take a user supplied minimum output and a deadline, and the contract must never hardcode zero or block.timestamp for those parameters.

title: Swap does not enforce a minimum output, exposing users to sandwich attacks
body: swapTokensForExactTokens forwards a minOut of zero to the router and has no deadline argument. An MEV searcher observing the pending transaction can front run it to move the pool, let the victim execute at the worse price, and back run to close the position, capturing the difference. Every swap path must take a user supplied minimum output and a deadline, and the contract must never hardcode zero or block.timestamp for those parameters.

title: transfer return value ignored for non-standard ERC20 tokens
body: The pool calls token.transfer and token.transferFrom without inspecting the boolean return value. Tokens such as USDT do not return a value at all, so the call reverts on a compiler generated return data check, while other tokens return false instead of reverting and the pool silently records a transfer that never happened. Route all token movement through the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 wrapper, which normalises both behaviours.

title: Flash loaned voting power lets an attacker pass a proposal in one block
body: castVote reads balanceOf at the moment of the call rather than a checkpointed balance at the proposal snapshot block. An attacker can flash borrow the governance token, vote with the borrowed weight, and repay in the same transaction at no cost. Voting weight must be read through the ERC20Votes getPastVotes accessor at a snapshot block chosen before the proposal was visible, and the execution delay must exceed the window in which the snapshot can be gamed.

title: Timelock executes queued calldata with delegatecall
body: The timelock forwards queued operations with delegatecall rather than call, so a scheduled proposal executes in the storage context of the timelock itself. A malicious or mistaken proposal can therefore overwrite the admin slot directly, bypassing the delay it was supposed to enforce. Use a plain call for external operations, and restrict delegatecall targets to an immutable allow list of audited libraries.

title: Liquidation can be blocked by a reverting receive function
body: liquidate pushes the seized collateral to the liquidator with a raw call and reverts if the call fails. A borrower who is also the counterparty of the liquidator, or a smart contract borrower with a reverting receive, can make every liquidation attempt revert and keep an underwater position open until the protocol accrues bad debt. Credit the proceeds to a withdrawable balance instead of pushing them, so a failing recipient cannot block the state transition.

title: Read only reentrancy on the Curve pool virtual price inflates collateral
body: The liquidation path reads get_virtual_price from the Curve pool while the pool is midway through remove_liquidity, a state in which the reentrancy lock of the pool is held but its view functions still return the stale, inflated value. This read only reentrancy lets an attacker borrow against collateral valued at a price that never existed on a settled block. Probe the pool lock by claiming remove_liquidity with a zero amount before trusting any of its view functions.

title: tx.origin used for authorisation allows phishing through an intermediary contract
body: The onlyOwner check compares tx.origin to the stored owner instead of msg.sender. If the owner is ever induced to call any function on an attacker controlled contract, that contract can call back into the protocol and pass the check, because tx.origin still refers to the owner. Authorisation must always be based on msg.sender; tx.origin has no legitimate use in access control.

title: Predictable randomness from blockhash and timestamp lets builders select winners
body: The mint function derives a rarity roll from the keccak256 hash of block.timestamp, block.prevrandao and msg.sender. All three inputs are visible to the builder assembling the block, so a searcher can simulate the call, discard unfavourable outcomes by reverting, and retry until a rare token is produced. Use a commit reveal scheme with a delay of several blocks, or a verifiable randomness service such as Chainlink VRF.

title: Storage layout collision after upgrade corrupts the owner slot
body: Version two of the implementation inserts a new uint256 field ahead of the existing owner declaration rather than appending it. Because the proxy retains the storage of version one, the new field reads the bytes that previously held the owner address and the owner variable now reads the old paused flag. Never reorder or insert state variables in an upgradeable contract: append only, and reserve a storage gap array in every base contract.

title: Unchecked block arithmetic underflows the vested amount
body: releasable computes vestedAmount minus released inside an unchecked block, added to save gas after the migration to Solidity 0.8. If released has been incremented by an admin correction and exceeds the recomputed vested amount, the subtraction wraps to an enormous number and the beneficiary can drain the escrow. Unchecked blocks are only safe where the invariant is proved on the line above; add an explicit comparison before the subtraction.

title: Withdrawal queue index reused after cancellation enables double claim
body: cancelWithdrawal deletes the request struct but leaves the queue index in the pending array of the user. A second call to claimWithdrawal reads the zeroed struct, whose amount field is zero, but the guard only checks that the index is present, so the shares are burned a second time against a request that no longer exists. Remove the index from the pending array on cancellation and assert that the request amount is non-zero before settling.

title: Operator can front run undelegation to avoid slashing
body: Slashing is applied when the challenge resolves, but undelegation takes effect immediately. An operator monitoring the mempool for a challenge transaction can submit an undelegation with a higher priority fee, exit the set before the slash lands, and keep the full stake. Undelegation must enter a queue whose delay exceeds the maximum challenge resolution window, and stake must remain slashable for the whole of that period.
